title: Exploring the Relationship Between Metacognitive and Collaborative Talk During Group Mathematical Problem-Solving https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14794802.2017.1410215
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page summarizes Smith and Mancy's study of how metacognitive and collaborative talk interact during group mathematical problem-solving among 9-10 year olds. The researchers coded student interactions to see whether metacognitive utterances tended to be preceded or followed by collaborative talk, and found a strong positive association between the two: collaborative talk raises the likelihood of metacognitive talk, and vice versa. This leads them to propose a new definition of collaborative metacognition, metacognition that emerges from the interplay of individual and group processes rather than from either alone. The summary notes that metacognitive interventions appear more effective on higher-reasoning-demand tasks and for lower-achieving students, suggesting teachers should tailor when and how they deploy explicit metacognitive prompts. It also flags the study's small sample size as a limitation, with the authors calling for further research.
points: Encouraging collaborative talk in group problem-solving increases the likelihood of metacognitive talk occurring, and metacognitive talk in turn tends to be followed by more collaboration; the two reinforce each other.
Metacognitive interventions appear to be more effective for lower-achieving students, suggesting they should be targeted rather than applied uniformly.
Teachers rarely see group-work skills develop automatically and need to explicitly teach students how to communicate, listen actively, and negotiate different perspectives.
Metacognitive prompts should be offered as an option students can choose to use, giving them ownership over developing their own self-regulation rather than imposing it.
quotes: This research article investigates the relationship between metacognitive and collaborative talk during group mathematical problem-solving among 9-10 year old students.

Their findings reveal a strong positive association between metacognitive and collaborative talk, suggesting that collaborative metacognition emerges from a combination of individual and group processes.

Teachers should understand the positive association between metacognitive talk and transactive (collaborative) talk. When students engage in collaborative talk, there is a higher probability of metacognitive talk occurring.
Interventions have also been shown to be more beneficial for lower-achieving students.
Collaborative metacognition is metacognition which can be identified as having contributed to, or arisen as a result of, group processes (or collaborative talk).
